rationale: A wins because it keeps three clean, structurally different stories and makes the proof burden do real work. Its strongest line, "Databricks claims $3B ARR and 60% growth - unaudited, on its own benchmarks, before any public filing," is a sharp accountability angle, even if "unaudited" needs backing. B has good material, but "the revenue figure and the IPO signal were disclosed alongside today's model release" invents timing the update did not give; that is how a decent angle becomes a correction waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: "unaudited" is stronger than the supplied facts. The update says Databricks is private and self-reporting; it does not establish audit status.
"Banks and hospitals want AI models they can audit" imports an audit frame that is plausible for regulated buyers but not explicitly in the update.
"beyond the press release" assumes the source format. The update says Databricks says the number; it does not say this came from a press release.
gaps_in_B: "the revenue figure and the IPO signal were disclosed alongside today's model release" invents a same-day IPO signal. The update only says Databricks has signaled an eventual IPO without a date.
Angles 2 and 3 over-slice the same regulated-enterprise story: "closed-API vendors' regulated customers" and "For banks and hospitals, the AI question is custody" need mostly the same customer proof.
"The reporter can test whether closed-API vendors are actually losing regulated accounts" is useful as a question, but the set risks implying churn evidence that is not in the update.
The next step, "pick one angle and resolve a real named reporter," punts on prioritization. A founder needs to know which proof to chase first, not admire four doors.
